key: We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into agreement with the obscurity of others.
s: The chapter counsels blunting sharp points, unravelling complications, tempering brightness and agreeing with the obscurity of others; the Heshang Gong commentary, on chapter 4, takes it as counsel to check the keen pursuit of merit and fame, following the Tao, which does not display itself, to untie knotted resentment, and to share the common dust rather than stand apart.

evidence.words: 人欲銳精進取功名，當挫止之，法道不自見也。…紛，結恨也。當念道無為以解釋。…當與眾庶同垢塵，不當自別殊。
evidence.gloss: (On blunting sharp points:) when a person wants to press keenly forward to seize merit and fame, he should check it and stop, modelling himself on the Tao, which does not display itself. (On unravelling complications:) complications are knotted resentments; one should think on the non-action of the Tao to untie them. (On agreeing with the dust:) one should share the grime and dust of the common people and not set oneself apart.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref Tao Te Ching 4, at [3]). The Heshang Gong base text 挫其銳，解其紛，和其光，同其塵 is the line of the key verse. Its comments carry each element of the reading: checking the keen pursuit of merit and fame after the Tao that does not display itself, untying knotted resentment, sharing the common dust rather than standing apart. Read the whole chapter; nothing contradicts. Plain sense restates the key verse faithfully. entry-check ok.
